title: Read-aloud off by default for proficient readers
statement: For fluent or upper-grade readers, as in Grade 9 literature, keep read-aloud of the text off by default but available on request, so reading time goes to unaided reading.
example: A review's evidence notes put the benefit of reading while listening at an effect size of about 0.06 when readers set their own pace.
detail: A review of a Grade 9 prototype made read-aloud the learner's choice and off by default, and kept word-by-word highlighting out of the default as a separate decision. Its evidence notes, which name no study, report a small overall benefit of reading while listening (g ≈ 0.18) that is largely a pacing artifact, one eye-tracking study in which text-to-speech disrupted proficient readers, and per-word highlighting that tested null against none in children with reading difficulties.
against: The notes limit the transfer to drama: "That literature is about prose, where speaker attribution is not a problem, so the general null does not straightforwardly transfer to multi-voice drama." (`g9/sources/Othello_1_Feedback_DevFactory.md`, line 403). The cited meta-analysis was mostly of college students (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/design/grade-9/research/learners-voice-guide.md`, line 87). Young readers are another case: a Grade 3 lesson design never gives the read-aloud up, since "Without the text there is no lesson." (`g9/library/text/L8d5159.txt`, lines 111 and 403), and Grade 3 keeps a read-aloud option throughout (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/rules/audio-and-voiceover.md`, line 193). A Grade 4 lesson keeps passage autoplay on as a deliberate hold against the guidance to stop it for older students, since turning it off before anyone knows what Grade 4 children actually do would trade a working lesson for an untested principle (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/content/lesson-plans/g4-u1-l1.json`, line 520; `grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/pedagogy/grade-4-vs-grade-3.md`, line 76; `grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/rules/audio-and-voiceover.md`, lines 204-205). A Grade 5 course keeps an explicit read-to-me or read-myself choice (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/g5-reading/review/start-here.md`, line 56), against a Grade 7 plan's claim that fading audio holds at every grade (`grade3-reading/edullm-review-hub/course-packages/courses/g7-reading/releases/2026-07-26/artifacts/Grade 7 Reading - BrainLift.md`, line 370). Another record lets a text read aloud in full sit above the learners' reading level. It rests on one review remark, not a measurement, and a performed audio version is still built for every speech (`othello-archive/scripts/play_audio.py`, line 1).

evidence.quote: Make read-aloud the student’s choice and off by default.
Do not pair audio with word-by-word highlighting by default. That is a separate decision.

The reading-while-listening literature gives a small overall benefit (g ≈ 0.18) which is largely a pacing artifact — experimenter-paced g ≈ 0.41 against self-paced g ≈ 0.06 — and one eye-tracking study found text-to-speech actively disrupted proficient readers.
Karaoke-style per-word highlighting tested null against no highlighting in children with reading difficulties.
Make read-aloud the student’s choice and off by default.

The reading-while-listening literature gives a small overall benefit (g ≈ 0.18) which is largely a pacing artifact — experimenter-paced g ≈ 0.41 against self-paced g ≈ 0.06 — and one eye-tracking study found text-to-speech actively disrupted proficient readers.
Make the audio available during the reading itself, not as a separate feature.
A meta-analysis of 57 studies, mostly with college students, compared three formats.
Spoken-plus-written was no better than written-only.
It beat spoken-only only for low-prior-knowledge learners, system-paced materials and materials without pictures.
Keep read-aloud as an opt-in tool for struggling or ELL readers.
For older students, the app should stop reading the text automatically, keeping audio for specific accessibility needs.
The guide's words matter far more than its face, and narrating text to fluent readers mostly does not help.
Grade 3 gets a read-aloud option throughout. For older students, the app should stop reading the text automatically, keeping audio for specific accessibility needs.
Note what this does not say: the audio still exists. What goes is the default.
### SPOV2 — Knowledge-first, no read-aloud crutch
Audio = pronunciation/gloss that fades; the transfer target is cold plain text.
